title: Module 1: Representations — Pixel, Patch and Location Embeddings

blocks.html:
What you will learn

  1. Load an AlphaEarth 64-D pixel embedding for one point
  2. Load a Clay 1024-D patch embedding for a nearby location
  3. Compare shape, spatial unit, temporal support and metadata side by side
  4. (Optional) Load a SatCLIP location embedding, if torch is installed
Prerequisite Needed?
Python, NumPy/pandas basics Yes
Earth Engine account No
torch No (optional, only for the SatCLIP section)

Time to complete: ~10 minutes.

Course reference environment: 2026-08 release. Provider APIs may change. Every cloud notebook has a local/offline fallback.

The AlphaEarth pixel vector

AlphaEarth (Google Satellite Embedding) produces one 64-D vector per 10 m pixel, per calendar year. It is a pixel embedding: the smallest spatial unit in this notebook, and the only one with a fixed annual cadence.

blocks.code:
bern = load("bern", 2024)
row = bern.iloc[0]
ae_vector = row[A_COLS].to_numpy(dtype="float32")
ae_norm = float(np.linalg.norm(ae_vector))

print("AlphaEarth pixel vector shape:", ae_vector.shape)
print("AlphaEarth pixel vector L2 norm:", round(ae_norm, 4))
print("Spatial unit: one 10m pixel")
print("Temporal support: one calendar-year composite (2024)")

blocks.html: Takeaway: the AlphaEarth vector is a single point in a 64-D space with no independently interpretable axis — see 01_alphaearth_access_visualize.ipynb for what that means visually.

The Clay patch embedding

Clay (via the LGND corpus) produces one 1024-D vector per Sentinel-2 L2A scene, per MajorTOM patch. It is a patch embedding: a much larger footprint than an AlphaEarth pixel, and tied to a single observation rather than a yearly composite.

blocks.after:
print("Clay patch embedding shape:", clay_vector.shape)
print("Clay patch embedding L2 norm:", round(clay_norm, 4))
print("Spatial unit: one Sentinel-2 patch (MajorTOM cell, 2,560 m)")
print("Temporal support: one Sentinel-2 L2A scene at", clay_row["datetime"])

with open("data/clay_sample_fixture.provenance.json") as f:
    clay_provenance = json.load(f)
print("Clay fixture provenance:", json.dumps(clay_provenance, indent=2))

Side-by-side comparison

Shape and spatial unit are the first two things to check before combining or comparing embeddings from different providers.

Optional: SatCLIP location embedding

SatCLIP produces a location embedding: it is derived from coordinates alone (lon/lat, sometimes with metadata like a target resolution), with no observation date at all. It knows nothing about what happened at a place this year — that is the tradeoff for needing no imagery to query it. SatCLIP requires torch, which is intentionally kept out of this course's core/providers install (ENV-05), so this section degrades gracefully when torch is absent.

blocks.code:
try:
    import torch  # noqa: F401

    TORCH_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
    TORCH_AVAILABLE = False

if not TORCH_AVAILABLE:
    print(
        "torch is not installed in this environment — skipping the SatCLIP "
        "section. SatCLIP location embeddings are optional per EARLY-02; "
        "see the isolated envs/clay/ environment referenced in the "
        "technology-stack docs for a torch-enabled walkthrough."
    )
else:
    # This branch is illustrative only: no bundled SatCLIP weights ship
    # with this course, so a real forward pass is out of scope here. It
    # is not expected to execute in the reference environment (torch is
    # absent by default) and does not need a real model checkpoint.
    satclip_vector = np.zeros(256, dtype="float32")  # placeholder shape only
    print(
        "torch is installed — SatCLIP location embeddings are typically a "
        "few hundred dimensions; placeholder shape:",
        satclip_vector.shape,
    )

blocks.html:
Wrap-up

  • The AlphaEarth vector is a single point in a 64-D space describing one 10 m pixel for one calendar year, with no independently interpretable axis.
  • A Clay patch embedding covers a much larger area and a single scene — "the same location" means something different for a pixel vector than for a patch embedding.
  • Shape and spatial unit are the first two things to check before combining or comparing embeddings from different providers.

What's next: 01_alphaearth_access_visualize.ipynb goes deeper on the AlphaEarth pixel embedding alone.

Resources:

  • AlphaEarth catalog: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/GOOGLE_SATELLITE_EMBEDDING_V1_ANNUAL
  • LGND / Clay v1.5 Sentinel-2 L2A corpus (Source Cooperative, CC BY 4.0): https://source.coop/clay/lgnd-clay-v1-5-sentinel-2-l2a
  • SatCLIP paper and repo: https://github.com/microsoft/satclip

quiz.prompt_html: You have a 64-D AlphaEarth vector for one point and a 1024-D Clay embedding for the same coordinates. Can you concatenate them into a single 1088-D vector and run cosine similarity against another such concatenated pair, expecting a meaningful result?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, since both are embeddings, concatenation is always safe.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the "Side-by-side comparison" section's Takeaway is explicit: "shape and spatial unit are the first two things to check before combining or comparing embeddings from different providers." A 10 m pixel and a 2,560 m patch describe physically different footprints; naive concatenation mixes incompatible spatial units.

options.label: B
options.text: No — not without first checking that the two embeddings describe the same spatial unit and temporal support, which for AlphaEarth (one 10 m pixel, one calendar-year composite) and Clay (one ~2,560 m MajorTOM patch, one Sentinel-2 scene) they do not.
options.explanation_html: Correct — this is exactly the comparison table in "Side-by-side comparison": dims, spatial_unit, and temporal_support differ, and the Takeaway names checking shape and spatial unit as the mandatory first step before combining providers.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because concatenating any two float32 arrays of any length is always mathematically valid.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — being programmatically possible (numpy will happily concatenate arrays) is not the same as being meaningful; the section's whole point is that shape compatibility does not imply semantic compatibility.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because Clay embeddings cannot be represented as numpy arrays.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the notebook does exactly that: clay_vector = np.array(clay_row["embedding"], dtype="float32") under "The Clay patch embedding" section, printing its shape as a normal array.

quiz.prompt_html: The AlphaEarth pixel vector print output shows shape (64,). What does this "one 10 m pixel" spatial unit mean when comparing two AlphaEarth vectors from points 5 meters apart?

options.label: A
options.text: They are almost certainly the same underlying 10 m pixel or immediately adjacent pixels, so high similarity between them says little beyond spatial adjacency.
options.explanation_html: Correct — "The AlphaEarth pixel vector" section states AlphaEarth is "the smallest spatial unit in this notebook" at "one 10 m pixel." Two points 5 m apart likely fall in the same or a neighboring pixel, so any similarity result mostly reflects that adjacency, not an independent land-cover judgment — the same adjacent-pixel leakage concern raised again in Module 3's spatial-CV section.

options.label: B
options.text: They must belong to different MajorTOM cells.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — MajorTOM cells are a Clay/LGND concept (2,560 m), described in "The Clay patch embedding" section, not an AlphaEarth pixel-level concept at all.

options.label: C
options.text: Their temporal support automatically differs, since AlphaEarth timestamps are pixel-specific.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — "The AlphaEarth pixel vector" section states AlphaEarth's temporal support is "one calendar-year composite (2024)," identical for every pixel drawn from the same year, not pixel-specific.

options.label: D
options.text: This has no bearing on interpretation; only the vector shape matters.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the section's Takeaway explicitly says the vector "with no independently interpretable axis" and points to spatial unit info printed alongside the shape, i.e., shape alone is insufficient.

quiz.prompt_html: The Clay patch embedding print output reports shape (1024,) and "Spatial unit: one Sentinel-2 patch (MajorTOM cell, 2,560 m)". A student claims: "since Clay's vector is bigger (1024 vs 64), it must describe a smaller, more precise spatial area than AlphaEarth." Is this correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, higher dimensionality always implies finer spatial resolution.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — dimensionality and spatial footprint are unrelated axes of comparison. The "Side-by-side comparison" table lists them as two separate columns (dims and spatial_unit) precisely because one does not determine the other.

options.label: B
options.text: No — the comparison table shows Clay's spatial unit is a 2,560 m MajorTOM cell, which is a much *larger* footprint than AlphaEarth's 10 m pixel, despite Clay's vector having many more dimensions.
options.explanation_html: Correct — this is stated directly in the "Side-by-side comparison" table and its Takeaway: Clay's spatial_unit is "one Sentinel-2 patch (MajorTOM cell, 2,560 m)" versus AlphaEarth's "one 10 m pixel" — the larger vector describes the larger area, the opposite of the student's claim.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because Clay is described as a "patch" embedding and patches are always smaller than pixels.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — "patch" in this course's vocabulary (see "The Clay patch embedding" heading) refers to a fixed MajorTOM tile, 2,560 m, larger than an AlphaEarth "pixel" (10 m), not smaller — the terms name spatial units, not implied sizes.

options.label: D
options.text: This cannot be determined from the notebook's output.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the "Side-by-side comparison" table prints exactly this information (spatial_unit column) for both providers.

quiz.prompt_html: What does the "Temporal support" field printed for AlphaEarth ("one calendar-year composite (2024)") versus Clay ("one Sentinel-2 L2A scene at [datetime]") tell you about matching them to the "same" point in time?

options.label: A
options.text: Both describe an identical, single-instant satellite pass, so temporal matching is straightforward.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the AlphaEarth vector is explicitly a "calendar-year composite," an aggregate over the whole year, not a single pass; the Clay vector is tied to "a single scene," a specific acquisition datetime — these are structurally different temporal supports, as the "The Clay patch embedding" Takeaway states directly: "means something different for a pixel vector than for a patch embedding."

options.label: B
options.text: AlphaEarth's yearly composite smooths over intra-year variation (e.g. seasonal change), while Clay's single-scene embedding reflects one specific date's conditions — so "the same year" does not mean "the same moment" across the two providers.
options.explanation_html: Correct — this is the direct reading of the two printed Temporal support lines and the section's Takeaway that "the same location" means something different for a pixel vector versus a patch embedding once you also account for time.

options.label: C
options.text: Temporal support is irrelevant to embedding comparison; only spatial unit matters.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the notebook prints both spatial unit and temporal support side by side in the comparison table specifically because both matter together, not just one.

options.label: D
options.text: Clay embeddings have no temporal information at all.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the print output explicitly shows clay_row["datetime"], a specific acquisition date, directly contradicting this option.

quiz.prompt_html: The "Optional: SatCLIP location embedding" section describes SatCLIP as a "location" embedding derived from coordinates alone, with no observation date. What is the key conceptual difference between a location embedding and the pixel/patch embeddings covered earlier?

options.label: A
options.text: Location embeddings require the most recent satellite pass to be computed.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the section states the opposite: SatCLIP "knows nothing about what happened at a place this year — that is the tradeoff for needing no imagery to query it," meaning it needs no recent (or any) imagery at query time.

options.label: B
options.text: A location embedding is derived purely from where a place is (lon/lat), not from what was observed there at any specific time — unlike AlphaEarth (annual composite) or Clay (single scene), both of which are grounded in actual satellite imagery.
options.explanation_html: Correct — this matches the section text directly: SatCLIP "is derived from coordinates alone... with no observation date at all," in contrast to the imagery-grounded pixel and patch embeddings covered in the earlier sections.

options.label: C
options.text: SatCLIP embeddings are always exactly 64-D, matching AlphaEarth.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the section's placeholder code explicitly uses np.zeros(256, dtype="float32") with the comment "placeholder shape only," and states real SatCLIP embeddings are "typically a few hundred dimensions" — not 64.

options.label: D
options.text: Location embeddings cannot be compared to pixel or patch embeddings under any circumstances.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the section doesn't make this absolute claim; it flags a conceptual tradeoff (no temporal grounding) rather than declaring comparison categorically impossible.

quiz.prompt_html: Why does the "Optional: SatCLIP location embedding" section wrap its demonstration in a try/except ImportError check for torch, rather than importing it unconditionally?

options.label: A
options.text: Because torch is intentionally kept out of this course's core/providers install, so the section must degrade gracefully when it is absent.
options.explanation_html: Correct — the section text states this directly: "SatCLIP requires torch, which is intentionally kept out of this course's core/providers install (ENV-05), so this section degrades gracefully when torch is absent."

options.label: B
options.text: Because torch is not a real Python package and the import would always fail.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — torch is a real, installable package; the code path that runs when TORCH_AVAILABLE is true demonstrates handling the case where it is installed.

options.label: C
options.text: Because SatCLIP cannot be described without running a live model.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — the section explicitly states the torch-available branch "is illustrative only... not expected to execute in the reference environment... does not need a real model checkpoint," i.e., no live model run is required either way.

options.label: D
options.text: Because import errors in Jupyter notebooks always crash the entire kernel.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect — Python's try/except ImportError is a standard, safe pattern precisely because it prevents a crash; that is the point of using it here.
